items.title: An MRI scanner uses a 1.5 tesla magnetic field — 30,000 times Earth's
items.claim: A typical clinical MRI scanner has a magnetic field around 1.5 T; high-field research machines reach 7 T. Generating such a field continuously requires kilometres of niobium-titanium wire cooled by liquid helium to about 4 K, where it becomes superconducting and carries current with no losses.
items.prompt: Why are superconducting magnets used instead of ordinary electromagnets?

options.text: An ordinary copper-wire electromagnet generating 1.5 T over the bore needed for a patient would dissipate megawatts of heat — practical only for brief pulses; a superconducting magnet, once energised, carries the same current forever with essentially no power input
Superconductors produce stronger fields per amp
Liquid helium is required for the radio detection

items.reveal:
A superconducting magnet is energised once (the current is ramped up from zero) and the current loop is closed via a superconducting switch. The current then flows indefinitely with no resistive losses. The magnet maintains its field as long as the helium keeps the wire below its critical temperature.

Liquid helium boils away slowly. A clinical MRI typically uses a 'cold head' refrigerator to recondense escaping helium — losses are then near zero for years. A 'quench' (loss of superconductivity, often from a tiny warm spot) dumps the magnet's stored energy as heat in seconds, boiling the helium and venting it through emergency pipes.

MRI uses the magnetic field to align protons in the patient's tissue; radio-frequency pulses tip the alignment; relaxation back to the field emits signals that are spatially reconstructed into images.
items.why: Superconductivity is taught as a cryogenic curiosity. It is the technology that makes medical MRI imaging possible — and many particle accelerators.

items.title: A pendulum trades potential and kinetic energy with no loss — in principle
items.claim: Pull a pendulum back to angle θ, release. At the bottom of the swing, all gravitational potential energy has become kinetic. Back at the top of the other side, all the kinetic energy is potential again. In an ideal frictionless pendulum, this swap continues forever.
items.prompt: Where does the energy actually go in a real pendulum?

options.text: It is destroyed at the bottom of the swing
Friction at the pivot, air resistance, and slight inelastic deformation of the string/rod all dissipate energy as heat. The amplitude decreases exponentially with each cycle (damped oscillation)
Energy is absorbed by Earth's gravitational field

items.reveal_title: Energy is conserved; the system simply transfers it out
items.reveal:
An ideal pendulum: m g L (1 - cos θ_max) of potential energy at the highest point becomes (1/2) m v² of kinetic energy at the bottom. The two trade places once per half-cycle.

A real pendulum loses some energy each cycle to friction at the pivot, drag through the air, and tiny inelastic effects in the string. The amplitude decays as exp(-t/τ) where τ is the time constant (typically minutes to hours for a good pendulum clock).

The pendulum's period for small angles is T = 2π√(L/g), independent of mass or amplitude. This is what made pendulum clocks accurate enough to be the global timekeeping standard from 1656 (Huygens) until ~1929 (when quartz oscillators overtook them).
items.why: Conservation of energy is taught as a static law. In a real oscillator it constrains where the energy goes — but it doesn't keep it all where you want it.
